newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon shelling raises questions over ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon shelling raises questions over ceasefire.

text.p: The shells that rained down on the city of Sidon and killed seven civilians fuelled fears that a 1996 ceasefire will be wrecked by spiralling violence in south Lebanon, analysts said on Tuesday.
"The fear from the shelling is that if this violence continues, the ceasefire will collapse and things will go haywire," said one Lebanese analyst.

Lebanese militiamen led by pro-Israeli commander Antoine Lahd shelled the southern port of Sidon on Monday after a roadside bomb blew up a car, killing two teenage children of a Lahd aide who himself died in a similar blast four years ago.
Israel, seeking to defuse Middle East tensions, distanced itself from the Sidon shelling and the roadside bomb which together killed a total of 10 civilians.

The shelling was the bloodiest attack on the Sidon area since Israeli forces mounted a 17-day offensive last year dubbed "Operation Grapes of Wrath" in which about 200 Lebanese civilians were killed in the south.
Under the terms of an April 1996 ceasefire that ended the onslaught, Israel and pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God) guerrillas agreed not to target civilians.
But pessimism about the pact has grown as increasing numbers of civilians have been caught up in cycles of violence in recent months.

Analysts said the shelling of Sidon also raised troubling questions about the fate of civilians in south Lebanon, who almost daily watch Israeli forces and Hizbollah guerrillas battle with rockets, roadside bombs and machineguns.

"Now everybody realises this violence is bound to continue until final peace in the region. We are trying to protect civilians. But civilians have become the ignitor," said Timor Goksel, spokesman for the United Nations Interim Forces in Lebanon (UNIFIL).
"At the end of the day in Lebanon, the only way to send messages is to hit the civilians and increase the pressure. But hitting civilians always brings a rough response," he told Reuters.
Hizbollah's answer to the Sidon shelling was dozens of Katyusha rockets that slammed into northern Israel early on Tuesday, wounding at least one civilian and causing some damage.
Goksel estimated that the radical Shi'ite group had fired about 80 rockets at Israel.
Hizbollah leaders have repeatedly vowed to unleash rocket attacks on Israel if Lebanese civilians continue to fall victim to Israel attacks.
And in a sign of rising tensions, the group on Tuesday departed from its usual caution when discussing rockets that land in Israel.

"The Islamic Resistance declares openly that it shelled the settlements in north occupied Palestine with a number of Katyusha rockets, causing many casualties," a Hizbollah spokesman in Beirut told Reuters.
In Sidon, Abdullah Qaseer, a Hizbollah deputy in parliament, said after visiting the wounded in hospitals:
"We are not going to accept any change in the equation which says the safety of civilians in Lebanon equals the safety of civilians in north Palestine."

Lebanese commentators said the Sidon shelling underscored wider concerns that the Israeli occupation of the south and the spasms of violence that come with it endanger Lebanon's drive to restore full stability following the 1975-1990 civil war.
"The preliminary results of the criminal shelling of Sidon are two victims -- the April understanding and internal stability," said an editorial in the conservative an-Nahar newspaper.
It is a commonly held belief that the strife in south Lebanon will ease only when comprehensive peace is reached in the Middle East.
In the meantime, analysts said, fresh bloodshed could be expected in the south as Hizbollah and Israeli forces braced for the next round of violence.
"The Sidon shelling may have just been an angry, emotional reaction to the roadside bomb," said one.
"But there is also the theory that the Israelis may be shifting their tactics by relying more on their militia allies. We will only be able to tell if there are more attacks like this one."
